card_quote: Myth exposure: met SPE and Milgram in intro psych, often without the critiques. / Narrative: Likes debunking content online; argues in group chats.
how_read: Dipped in. Went straight to round 3 (the psych experiments) and round 4 in one sitting because that's my stuff, then went back and did round 1, then skimmed rounds 5 and 6 over the week between problem sets. Didn't get past the physics round before midterms took over.

w1_friction.note: Newton's apple, then Newton's apple again. Same sources even.
w1_friction.quote: Newton himself told of the apple, according to Britannica

w1_friction.note: Every answer says 'the record' like I'm supposed to know what record. Is it a database? A court record? Reads a bit like an AI summarizing Wikipedia.
w1_friction.quote: The data tell a weaker story.

w1_friction.note: The 65% literally happened in the baseline condition, the book says so. The number's right, it's the interpretation that's disputed. Calling the question DISPUTED feels like a technicality.
w1_friction.quote: About 65 percent of participants went to the maximum 450 volts

w1_friction.note: By now every answer has the exact same beats: popular version, the record, why it spread, safe statement. I could write the next one myself.
w1_friction.quote: The stronger version spread partly through that pair of figures.

w1_friction.note: Pretty sure forgetting curves have been measured on loads of people since Ebbinghaus in spaced-repetition research. 'Based on one person' is true about the origin but kind of a gotcha.
w1_friction.quote: The forgetting curve rests on one subject

w1_friction.note: Two number 31s? And this one says Discovery Stories in the Charts round.
Verdict says TRUE, first line says it's a later embellishment, last line says he never flew it. Lol what. Also one Wikipedia link when every other page has journal refs.
w1_friction.quote: The kite flight in a storm is a later embellishment.

w1_friction.note: Wald's planes again right after Wald's planes. Should've been one entry.
w1_friction.quote: The reasoning in the famous story is Wald's.

w1_friction.note: Monty Hall. Everyone who has taken stats has done this one to death.
w1_friction.quote: Switching wins two times in three.

w1_friction.note: Laffer napkin, then Laffer again. Third repeat pair I've hit.
w1_friction.quote: Arthur Laffer has disclaimed originality for the curve

w1_friction.note: Why is a question about Eskimo words in the physics round? I skipped the round intro so this threw me.
w1_friction.quote: DO ESKIMO LANGUAGES HAVE FAR MORE WORDS FOR SNOW THAN ENGLISH?

w1_best.why: We literally got taught Stanford prison as fact in intro psych with zero mention of the coaching. Sending this to the group chat.
The 2026 Dawson and de Meza reanalysis where it inverts is new to me. Best 'well actually' in the book.
'Entirely fictional' from Levitt and List. Great quote, short story, solid source.
Mount Stupid not being in the paper. Everybody posts that chart.
Two-thirds independent, not caving. Nice clean number flip that would win a trivia round.

w1_flat.why: Contradicts itself and is clearly a different, lazier write-up than the rest.
Same Wald story as the page before, just the other half.
Second Laffer entry. Felt like filler.
Monty Hall is the most overplayed puzzle there is.

w1_review.headline: Good takedowns of the psych classics, padded with repeats
w1_review.body: Rounds 3 and 4 are legit: Stanford prison, Hawthorne, Asch and Dunning-Kruger all get the critiques my textbook skipped, with real papers cited. But the writing follows the same template every time, a bunch of stories are basically asked twice, and there's a Franklin page that says TRUE and then says it never happened. Bottom line: borrow it or get it for your nerdy dad, read rounds 3 and 4, skip the rest.

w2_review_first: I'd say if you like debunk videos, the psych section is actually good and has stuff I hadn't seen, like the new Dunning-Kruger reanalysis. But it's long-winded, it repeats itself, and I wouldn't pay much for it.

w2_lost.why: Wald's planes for the second time. That's where I first got the 'wait, didn't I just read this' feeling.
Monty Hall. I already know it, so I skipped ahead.
Laffer twice. Put it down after that one for a few days.
The physics round. Coriolis and sinks is a YouTube classic and midterms started, so that was it.

w2_read_aloud.why: It's the one everyone at the table thinks they know, and they're wrong.
The 'entirely fictional' line lands out loud.
Toast actually being studied by a physicist sounds fake, so it's perfect for a guessing game.
Rat-catchers cutting tails off live rats. People would lose it.
Six downloads before the lawsuit. Great number to drop at trivia.

w2_cut.why: From the title alone, the goldfish memory thing is the most overdone fact on the internet.
Merge it with the other Wald one.
Merge it with the other Laffer one.
Merge it with the other Newton one.

w2_book2: If it's another hundred where like fifteen are the same story asked twice and half of them I already saw on YouTube.
